title: How the Economic Case for International Students Lost Steam
content:
W ith widespread delays holding up tens of thousands of foreign students worldwide from getting their visas, the “U.S. economy could suffer a loss of $7 billion,” a higher-education group warned recently.

A precipitous drop in international enrollments wouldn’t just be bad for colleges, it would be a blow to the larger economy, NAFSA: Association of International Educators admonished. Not only would tuition not be paid, plane tickets wouldn’t be booked, apartments wouldn’t be rented, and dorm-room refrigerators wouldn’t be stocked. Across the country, 60,000 jobs could be lost.

Arguments that emphasize the economic impact of international students are intended to resonate beyond campuses. What’s more, they would appear tailor-made for the country’s businessman-in-chief, who has prioritized cutting government costs and spurring economic growth.

If you don’t live in a hub for international students, “the economic argument loses its salience.”

Yet such messaging seems to be falling on deaf ears. The Trump administration has chided Columbia University for its “financial dependence” on international students. It has castigated Harvard for treating foreign students as a “giant cash cow” and attempted to boot the university from the student-visa system.

As the White House imposes punishing tariffs on America’s trade partners, education — with which the United States has a trade surplus with almost every country in the world — hasn’t been part of negotiations. The administration has threatened a 145-percent trade penalty on Chinese goods while also vowing to “aggressively revoke” the visas of students from China, a group that spends more than $14 billion annually to study here.

The “irony seems to be lost on President Trump,” said Dany Bahar, director for migration, displacement, and humanitarian policy at the Center for Global Development. “One of his signature goals, narrowing the trade deficit, is actively undermined” by his foreign-student policies.

Those policies could be bad news for colleges’ bottom lines. Many fear that new visa restrictions and attacks on colleges by President Trump and his allies could damage American higher education’s global reputation and sink international enrollments.

To the sector’s dismay, the broader public also appears unmoved by what has long been a winning case. The arguments for enrolling international students may be falling out of vogue, while the arguments against it grow in popularity. In an America First moment, the politics of immigration seem to trump the economics of overseas tuition. And among Americans skeptical, or even hostile, to higher education — well, they just might not be willing to buy colleges’ reasoning.

“The economic case for international students is increasingly falling flat in today’s climate for almost everyone,” said Chris R. Glass, a professor of educational leadership and higher education at Boston College. “In my view, the economic-impact argument is ineffective and even counterproductive.”

L et’s get this out of the way: The evidence that international students are an economic plus is abundant. Both NAFSA and the federal government publish annual calculations of international students’ financial impact. The U.S. Department of Commerce considers education one of the country’s top service exports, bigger than coal and corn, about equal to what American carmakers earn overseas.

ADVERTISEMENT

Foreign students who pay full freight subsidize their domestic classmates and help colleges make up for funding cuts and other lost revenue. After China joined the World Trade Organization 24 years ago, Chinese families spent their new income on American degrees, research shows, setting international-enrollment records.

A new trade war “risks unraveling the United States’ competitive advantage,” said Gaurav Khanna, an associate professor of economics at the University of California at San Diego and an author of the report.

The influx of tuition dollars from China, India, and elsewhere over the last two decades coincided with a shift away from the way colleges had traditionally described the value of international students, which emphasized how the students added to campuses’ cultural diversity. In fact, higher education as a whole was being repositioned in terms of the return on investment: as a driver of local economies and as a necessity for graduates to secure a place in the middle class.

“It’s the argument that resonated” with the American public, said Brendan Cantwell, a professor of higher, adult, and lifelong education at Michigan State University. International education’s true believers might be enthusiastic about the expanded world view and deeper cultural understanding foreign students brought to campus. But many parents cared less about their kids having a roommate from another country than about their getting a credential for the job market at a good price — without necessarily realizing that foreign students helped keep the costs of that degree lower.

ADVERTISEMENT

Some colleges started to make that argument to parents and to lawmakers anxious about tuition increases. Hometown business owners, meanwhile, made the connection that an influx of international students meant new markets for restaurant meals, winter coats, and flashy cars.

Still, Alan Ruby, a senior fellow at the Graduate School of Education at the University of Pennsylvania, said there have always been limitations to this line of thinking. After all, the 1.1 million international students, and their $44 billion in economic impact, aren’t distributed evenly throughout the United States but instead are concentrated in college towns and big cities. Of the 10 colleges with the largest international populations, two each are in Boston and New York City, with two more in California. Only three are in states won by Trump last year.

The economic activity of international students at the 10th ranked institution, the University of North Texas, is equal to all the dollars foreign students spend in Oklahoma, according to NAFSA data; in 18 other states, foreign students spent less. Students from overseas at New York University, which has both the highest enrollments of such students and the greatest economic impact from them, generated more dollars than all but eight states.

If you don’t live in a hub for international students, “the economic argument loses its salience,” Ruby said.

If the economic argument for international enrollments has lost its oomph, what else is likely to be compelling?

The case can also be muddied by the breadth and diversity of the American economy. Higher education is a multibillion-dollar export — but so too are aircraft parts, pharmaceuticals, and financial services. “Arguments about aggregate economic impact are a lot more abstract,” Ruby said, “than ‘what have you done for me lately.’”

In other countries, foreign students’ jolt to the economy may be more visible. In Australia, for example, education is among the top-five exports. And international students make up about a third of all Australian university students compared with just 6 percent of total enrollments at American colleges.

ADVERTISEMENT

Most American colleges aren’t “truly dependent” on international students, said Philip G. Altbach, founding director of the Center for International Higher Education at Boston College, which can undercut assertions about just how essential they are.

E ven if American colleges were relying on international students to keep the lights on, it’s not clear that would be a winning argument.

Trump, in fact, has tried to wield the tuition revenue that colleges like Harvard and Columbia do get against them, painting their advocacy of international students as self-interested. Bringing up the economic impact of foreign students “sounds like a self-serving talking point,” said Glass, the educational-leadership professor at Boston College. And so it backfires, feeding resentments held by Americans who are already angry at higher education — for its high costs and role as an economic gatekeeper, for its liberalism and elitism.

When a post by Glass about declining international enrollments recently went viral on social media, many of the responses crowding his mentions were celebratory. They thanked him, he said, for “sharing the good news.’”

ADVERTISEMENT

Debates over international students may not just be influenced by polarization about higher education but colored by people’s views on globalization and, by extension, colleges’ global engagement. Trump has seized on the very real dislocation caused by the global economy to campaign and now govern on a blueprint that pits Americans against outsiders, us versus them. Immigrants, foreigners, and even international students have been the targets of policies such as visa revocations, migrant detentions, and a travel ban. The economic good of international students may not be able to transcend the politics of the moment.

If the economic argument for international enrollments has lost its oomph, what else is likely to be compelling?

Rather than focusing on short-term financial gains, advocates for foreign students — who are the majority of doctoral students in critical STEM fields — could foreground their importance to longer-term American competitiveness and innovation, Glass said, a tactic international-education groups have also pursued.

Or the economic message could be more persuasive from a different messenger. In 2020, during Trump’s first term, a group of local and state governments supported a lawsuit brought by colleges challenging a policy that would have required foreign students to return to in-person classes during the pandemic. Forcing students to leave the country would be a blow to their economies, the government officials argued. (The rule was soon rescinded.)

ADVERTISEMENT

Fanta Aw, NAFSA’s executive director and chief executive, said that when her organization released its estimate of the effects of a sharp decline in international enrollments this fall, they had an audience beyond the White House in mind. The group highlighted the impact on a state-by-state basis and is working with educators across the country to share the data locally. If the visa backlog isn’t dealt with soon, municipal leaders won’t need a spreadsheet to calculate the costs to their community, Aw fears.

In the end, it’s the personal narrative, not the dollars and cents, that will create a sense of urgency, she said. “The economic argument is exactly the right argument, but we have to zero in on the who.”

title: When the Legislature Kills Your Department
content:
S weeping reviews of whether to keep or ditch smaller academic programs have become a staple of college operations in the last decade thanks to mounting financial pressures. But they’ve always been initiated by leaders at the campus, or maybe at the system, level as a reaction to strained budgets or a perceived need to shake up curricula. And they have always been deeply unpopular with many professors, who bear the brunt of their impact.

This spring, a handful of states — Indiana, Ohio, and Utah — have written academic-program reviews into law for the first time, making them mandatory for public colleges statewide.

This goes against decades of institutional policy and practice at most colleges, where professors have played the key role in developing, approving, and maintaining curricula. Faculty curation of academic programs is required by accrediting agencies. Academic programs may be subject to review and termination by institutional leadership for financial reasons, but the process is often fraught, and the results have a way of being shifted by department mergers and other factors. In 2021, for example, the University of Vermont eliminated eight majors months after initially announcing it planned to end 12 majors and 11 minors.

For faculty members and other critics, the new laws represent yet another conservative overreach and a threat to shared governance and academic freedom. Proponents of the laws and some other observers see them as a way to hold colleges more accountable for the public dollars they spend and the subjects they teach.

Indiana and Ohio have set enrollment thresholds below which an academic program is subject to possible termination: In Indiana , 15 or fewer students majoring; in Ohio , fewer than five degrees conferred annually over any three-year period. In Utah, the law doesn’t mention enrollment thresholds at all but predicates a successful program review on factors such as meeting work-force needs and institutional mission.

Laws mandating academic-program reviews have no precedent, says John Lane, vice president for academic affairs at the State Higher Education Executive Officers Association (SHEEO). But they are not without roots. The authority for academic programs at public colleges ultimately comes from the state. Elected officials have often expressed concerns in recent years about the efficiency of academic programs, Lane says: “I see this more as a degree of that, a crescendo, as opposed to something new that’s happening.”

And program reviews can be good for a college, says Paul N. Friga, a clinical professor of strategy and entrepreneurship at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill and a consultant who works with other colleges. “Many institutions in higher education are inert,” he says. “They’ve done things a long, long time a certain way, and it’s uncomfortable to switch things up. So sometimes you need an outside force to get different results.” If state legislators — or the board of trustees at a private college — are unhappy with the way things are going at their institutions, he adds, they’re going to want to influence more decisions.

Even some advocates of the laws acknowledge that the optics aren’t ideal. Sure, states provide financial support for public colleges — in Ohio, it was $2.8 billion in fiscal year 2024, according to SHEEO. It’s not unreasonable for Ohio lawmakers to believe they “should play a larger role in how we’re making these investments in higher education,” says Greg Lawson, a research fellow at the Buckeye Institute, a think tank dedicated to Ohio politics.

Still, “this is a little bit on the heavy-handed side,” says Lawson, whose institute lobbied on behalf of the legislation. While he says he’d like to see colleges evaluate programs more explicitly based on outcomes rather than enrollment, he thinks it’s a sound law.

F or some lawmakers and proponents of the program-review laws, it’s a matter of simple math. Public-college systems in many states were built to accommodate the enrollment bonanza of the Baby Boom and its wake and now serve populations with a waning number of traditional-age students. Meanwhile, state budgets remain snug almost everywhere. Ohio is home to 14 public four-year universities, many with branch campuses, and 22 community colleges. “Now the question is,” says Lawson, “are we a little top-heavy with, maybe, institutions, but more relevantly, individual programs?” Every four-year campus having its own French major, say, may comport with the classic definition of a university, but what’s to be done if French departments across the state have trouble staying full while more work-force-oriented majors overflow with students?

What Will Trump’s Presidency Mean For Higher Ed? Keep up to date on the latest news and information, and contact our journalists covering this ongoing story.

Public colleges must look to the future, says Jeff Raatz, a Republican state senator in Indiana and chair of the Senate Committee on Education and Career Development. If there are disciplines that have few majors now, because of lack of interest from students or limited career paths, “it’s a necessary exercise for schools to take a look at what they’re doing and understand that — with what we know is going to happen with the low birth rates in this country — what does that look like three years from now, or four years or five years?” They must figure out how to be proactive, he says.

Some lawmakers may be perplexed by, or even resent, some aspects of higher education, but they can’t deny its importance to things they care about — especially work-force development. That helped keep the program-review law in Utah from being more severe.

ADVERTISEMENT

Utah’s new program-review law was born when the Republican-dominated legislature let it be known that members were contemplating a straightforward cut to state support for public colleges, according to Geoffrey Landward, commissioner at the Utah System of Higher Education. “It was clear that there was just a lack of trust” between legislators and state colleges, he says. “They did not view us as partners. They viewed us as a problem.” Lawmakers were frustrated, he adds, that they had sunk money into higher education — $1.9 billion in fiscal year 2024, according to SHEEO — and had no say in what kind of return they got on their investment. “I don’t think it’s any secret, especially in a red state, that a lot of this frustration was ideological,” Landward says, “seeing, in their view, politically controversial, if not contrary, points of view being taught, researched, advocated for.”

Landward and others began discussions with legislators to avoid a cut and mollify concerns about public colleges. “Everybody agreed that the role that higher education plays in the prosperity of the state is significant and cannot be ignored,” Landward says. From that point, he says, the question was whether to disinvest or to think more strategically about how to invest.

In Utah’s program-review law, majors will be evaluated on a variety of factors, including student demand, work-force needs, outcomes (including salary), how important they are to the institution’s mission, and “other criteria.” Eventually Utah lawmakers acknowledged that “it can’t be a simple, binary approach — you’re either enrolling or you’re not,” Landward says. “Everybody agreed that making a determination of what makes a program a high-value, high-performing program should be and is a complicated question, and that there isn’t one equation to just come up with a number based on several inputs and say, This is a cut program, or this is a keep program.” For example, graduates in social work often receive relatively low pay, Landward notes, but the state needs social workers, so the program couldn’t be penalized too much for lower salaries after graduation.

Public-college leaders in Utah, not legislators, will oversee the reviews and make recommendations about programs to cut or merge with other programs. Proposals will be subject to final approval by the Legislature, however, which will also apportion funds for new programs.

ADVERTISEMENT

A cademic-program reviews may be conducted in a variety of ways or with varying enrollment metrics. But critics of the laws suspect many of the majors on the chopping block will be liberal-arts areas already under scrutiny at other institutions, including classic humanities subjects such as philosophy, foreign languages, and identity-based disciplines like gender studies. Many such programs have neither the number of student majors nor the direct connection to jobs that programs in health care or business do. Proponents of program-review laws say that’s not why they’re up for review. “I had a phone call from someone who said, ‘Are you trying to deliberately eliminate the liberal arts in schools in Indiana?’” says Raatz. “Absolutely not. That was never even part of the thought process.”

In Utah, it’s not clear yet how the program reviews will affect what public colleges offer. There was significant concern, both in the Legislature and within the state university system, that “we don’t even know what this is going to look like,” Landward says. “This is us being good stewards of taxpayer money, but at the same time, no one wants to live in a society where we have no liberal arts, where we have no humanities.”

An outline of the University of Utah’s plan, presented to the Utah Board of Higher Education in June, includes a list of 94 academic programs to be “sunsetted.” The greatest number — 27 — are in the College of Humanities, though 18 come from the College of Science and 11 from the College of Engineering.

Even when programs do close, Landward hopes that the system can make up for some here or there through course sharing. For example, foreign-language majors showed up on virtually every institution’s plan. “From a work-force standpoint, it’s hard to connect the dots and say, This is a high-performing program,” he says. But in Utah, thanks to the presence of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter Day Saints, foreign languages are critical: Many Mormons go on proselytizing missions overseas. “Let’s look at this being offered across the state, not by every institution, but by one, in partnership with other institutions,” Landward says. The students need access to language programs, he adds, “but do we need to recreate the infrastructure of language programs at every university? No, we don’t.”

ADVERTISEMENT

But elected officials are running a risk, says Lawson, if they emphasize academic programs that lead to jobs right after graduation over the “soft skills” imbued by a traditional liberal-arts education that may also be valuable in the workplace. “If we become so focused that we’re only doing things that we know are going to turn out students that are inherently employable,” he says, “are we creating the right critical-thinking skills, are we helping folks get what they need to be good, well-rounded citizens? I think there’s going to be an interesting kind of push-pull dynamic in that space.”

M any faculty members are less sanguine about the new academic-program-review laws. According to Felecia Commodore, an associate professor of education policy, organization, and leadership at the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign, they amount to an attack on academic freedom and shared governance — two of the key pillars of American higher education for decades — in large part by removing professors from the process of determining curriculum. “We’ve had concerns about what’s being taught in our classrooms before,” she says, “but I don’t know that we’ve ever had a movement to legalize that scrutiny.”

Especially in Indiana, the academic-program-review law is part of a series of moves in recent years to attack higher education and “disembowel the faculty,” says Christopher A. Lubienski, a professor of education policy at Indiana University at Bloomington. Last-minute additions to a budget bill this spring, for example, introduced a post-tenure-review process for faculty members and officially made shared governance “advisory only.” “There are definitely arguments for paying attention to programs that are not being fully utilized,” he says. “But I’m quite concerned about the state coming in and mandating this, setting actual specific numbers to determine program minimum requirements, because that’s typically not been their area.”

Kendall Gerdes, an associate professor of writing and rhetoric studies at the University of Utah and head of the institution’s chapter of the American Association of University Professors, can’t swear that no faculty members were directly involved in the deliberations over programs to be cut there, but she doesn’t know of any. She considers the law part of an ongoing effort to erode shared governance in the state’s public colleges. “Erring on the side of transparency would be a lot more healthy for making deliberative decisions about this stuff together,” Gerdes says. “But that’s not what my university has chosen to do.”

ADVERTISEMENT

A university spokesperson said faculty members were involved throughout the process through town halls and other meetings designed to solicit input, and provosts were engaged in all stages of the decision-making.

Commodore believes that, despite any rhetoric about institution-level efficiency or enrollment, the laws are a sign of anti-higher-ed attitudes from the Trump administration starting to filter down from the federal level to the states, which exercise direct control of public colleges. She points, as another example, to two recent bills in North Carolina that would have banned “diversity, equity, and inclusion” and “divisive concepts” in state government only to be vetoed by Josh Stein, the Democratic governor. “If someone has an idea about how our society should run, what it should or shouldn’t do, we use the process of lawmaking to formalize that,” she says. “Even if we believe something has just been ideological conversations, when those conversations are being had by legislators, we need to pay attention, because those ideologies become laws.”

The laws are affecting professors in more-direct ways, too, sowing uncertainty and anxiety. Matthew R. Hotham, for example, was an associate professor of religious studies at Ball State University, in Muncie, Ind., until early July. Now he’s a member of the institution’s history department, at least for the time being. The religious-studies department at Ball State had perhaps 20 students majoring in it, not enough to meet the threshold for the Indiana statute, as the university’s leaders interpreted it. So Hothman knew that his discipline was probably on the block. He and the department’s only other remaining full-time faculty member had already been talking to the history department about a merger for a couple of years before the law passed, so the switch to a new academic home isn’t too discomfiting.

Hotham isn’t sure what happens further down the road, though. The university’s accreditor still has to sign off on the merged departments. He notes that the text of the law calls for the elimination of underenrolled programs and “any costs associated” with them. He’s been asked to participate in recruiting events and will be teaching in the fall, he says, but “I’m not sure that that’ll be true in the fall of 2026.” A spokesperson for Ball State declined to comment for this article.

ADVERTISEMENT

What is certain is that some elected officials have reached the end of their patience with higher education. Academic freedom is “sometimes an argument that doesn’t really resonate well with a lot of legislators,” says Landward, the Utah system head who spent months negotiating with lawmakers over the shape of that state’s program-review law. “There’s a difference between academic freedom and the notion that we have absolute freedom to do whatever we want with the money that we’re given.”

Landward acknowledges that program reviews in Utah will lead some professors to lose their jobs. But he also has a vision of a possible future that benefits both the state’s public colleges and the state itself. By cutting back on underperforming programs, he says, the system will be able to invest more in growing disciplines, which should encourage economic growth.

There is another vision of the future that could coexist right alongside that — one in which these laws could narrow students’ options and horizons. Some students will arrive on campus these days uncertain what they want to study; once they do arrive, they may have trouble understanding or studying the full scope of academic options. “Sometimes you don’t know that it’s there to be pursued or thought about unless you see it in place already,” says Lane, of SHEEO. “If we are reducing some of those programs, it raises the question, Will this impose limitations on students’ aspirations?”

title: A ‘Nightmare’: Alums and Retirees Say the Loss of Their College Inboxes Feels Personal
content:
When Russell Bryant was given his @temple.edu email address as a freshman in 2010, administrators assured him that he would have the account for life. So after graduation, he used the email for all sorts of things: Apple Pay, Spotify, his electricity bills, and more.

Then, late last year, Temple University said that it would discontinue university email access for all alumni who had graduated more than a year before.

“I was really just taken aback,” said Bryant.

Bryant, now a real-estate lawyer, decided to take his alma mater to court.

“I’ve been using it for over 15 years, and the email address is tied to so many different (things),” he said. "… It’s really a significant part of my everyday life.”

This past year, several other colleges, including Vanderbilt and Wright State Universities, have also terminated the email accounts of thousands of alumni and retirees in response to cyberthreats and changes in Google’s storage policies.

For administrators, maintaining thousands of alumni and retiree email accounts is costly and poses a high risk with little return, since so few people actually use the accounts.

At Vanderbilt, for example, where administrators announced they would terminate alumni email accounts this summer, they said fewer than 15 percent are used monthly.

The number of ransomware attacks has skyrocketed in higher education since Covid-19, when colleges increased their reliance on remote work.

One of the primary culprits is email, in which ever-more sophisticated phishing attacks blend in with routine messages about campus goings-on, a 2024 analysis found. By tricking users into downloading malware or sharing login or financial information, hackers can obtain sensitive student and employee data, research information, and financial records and hold them for ransom. That can be financially damaging for a college. It can also shut down a campus’s entire operations for days or weeks at a time.

Ed Hudson, the vice chancellor of information technology at the University of Kansas, said it’s become more and more difficult to fend off email hacks as the number of alumni and retirees grows.

“When you’re here, we’re able to support that population more effectively, and we have a better handle on the platforms that they’re using,” Hudson said. “But when you leave, we lose that ability and that insight into what you’re doing, and that increases risk.”

ADVERTISEMENT

Because alumni and retirees are no longer beholden to university policies, administrators can’t enforce information-security standards.

Hudson said assurances administrators gave that email addresses would remain with alumni and retirees for life were probably based on information available to them at the time.

“The intent back then and the threats that we had back then were different,” Hudson said.

Josh Stein, a 2012 alumnus of Vanderbilt University, has used his alumni email to send out countless resumes. Vanderbilt, citing cybersecurity risks, announced this spring it planned to discontinue alumni access to Google Workspace later this month.

ADVERTISEMENT

Vanderbilt is one of several colleges that used Google Workspace for Education to provide students, alumni, and faculty members with university email addresses. Google announced in 2021 it would phase out free unlimited data-storage plans for colleges and universities.

“The nightmare is really all the unknown stuff,” said Stein, who graduated with a degree in computer science and mathematics and works in the software-engineering industry. He’s concerned about losing potential professional opportunities and connections.

“The real problem is, what about all of the résumés that I’ve sent out over my 20 years that have landed in some database for either a recruiter or an institution, and those people now don’t have a good way to reach me. There’s no real way for me to go back and figure out every single place that I’ve ever applied to,” Stein said.

“All of my [stuff] is entangled under this email,” he said. When he was a student, “they actively encouraged us to go wild with the unlimited storage perk, and having it for life. It was like, OK, I can trust them. They’re an institution. Of course they will fulfill their obligations, right?”

Stein can’t help but feel slighted.

“I use their email address and I think of myself ... as a steward of that label,” Stein said of Vanderbilt. “That was a decision they had entrusted to me at the time, which made me feel good. … I’m going to work hard for you at your school. You give me this trust, and you’re going to have me carry this torch, basically forever. Walking that back and saying ‘never mind’ 20 years later, it’s a sting.”

ADVERTISEMENT

Wright State University’s decision this spring to eliminate retirees’ email accounts was catastrophic to Robin Suits. As webmaster of the Wright State University Retirees Association, Suits uses a mailing list of 600 active .edu email addresses belonging to retirees to keep the organization’s members connected and up to date, including information about its annual luncheon, the passing of former faculty members, and renovations on campus.

“We anticipate that it will be devastating to our organization,” Suits said. “And we’ve been very active — we have events throughout the year, and we just feel like it’s going to be really bad.” Since May, only 20 members have updated their contact information. Suits, who has petitioned Wright State administrators to reverse their decision, said she might be forced to rely solely on the U.S. Postal Service for the group’s communication in the future.

Bryant, the lawyer and Temple grad, said after The Philadelphia Inquirer wrote about his lawsuit, dozens of other alumni asked to join his legal action. Bryant’s effort to turn his case into a class-action lawsuit was denied on a technicality, but the “overwhelming” support he received boosted his resolve.

“It really kept me going and putting my foot down to try to make this happen for everybody,” he said.

title: Under Pressure From Trump, the Accreditor Overseeing Harvard Proposes Nixing DEI Standards
content:
What’s New

The accreditor that oversees Harvard University said Friday that it’s considering removing language from its standards that refers to diversity, equity, and inclusion.

The New England Commission of Higher Education — which accredits more than 200 colleges, primarily in the Northeast — is one of several major institutional accreditors that are reconsidering if and how members should demonstrate how they’re meeting diversity goals.

The commission’s members were concerned about potential conflicts between the accreditor’s standards and declarations from the federal government that DEI measures are illegal, said Lawrence M. Schall, president of the commission.

The Trump administration has put intense pressure on both accreditors and their member colleges, including the New England commission in particular. In a June letter, the Departments of Health and Human Services and Education told the accreditor that it had found Harvard in violation of civil-rights law, and that action may be required because the university “may no longer meet” accreditation standards. (The commission has acknowledged to the departments that it received that notice, Schall said, and explained its process for responding to the issue.)

On Wednesday, the Department of Justice directed federally funded institutions to abandon any effort to rectify racial disparities in academic outcomes. The new guidance also suggested that efforts to target student recruitment in historically underserved communities could be using geography as an illegal proxy for race.

“What we heard from institutions is that they felt they would be put in an untenable position,” Schall said, especially the U.S. military academies that are accredited by the commission and bound by law to follow the president’s executive orders.

The commission’s members include the U.S. Coast Guard Academy and the U.S. Naval War College, as well as the Ivy League’s Yale University, which is facing heightened scrutiny over allegations that it is violating civil-rights laws.

The Details

The New England commission’s current standards include references to diversity, equity, and inclusion under five of the nine major areas it measures, including organization and governance, students, and institutional resources.

ADVERTISEMENT

Under the guidelines for serving students, for example, the standard states: “The institution addresses its own goals for the achievement of diversity, equity, and inclusion among its students and provides a safe environment that fosters the intellectual and personal development of its students.”

The suggested changes would require the college to respond to “the needs of its student population,” provide “support services,” and make “provisions for responding to them including strategies for having all students feel welcomed, supported, and included in the community.”

In the current framework, the commission doesn’t actually require its members to pursue diversity, equity, and inclusion, Schall emphasized. But if colleges do have that goal, the standard frames how they should present it during the accreditation process.

“If you have goals around diversity, equity, inclusion, we would like to know what they are and be updated on the progress you’re making to meet them,” Schall said in an interview, “but we don’t require any school to have a DEI plan.”

ADVERTISEMENT

Overall, the draft changes articulate a more streamlined approach, Schall said, that provides colleges more flexibility in meeting the accreditor’s requirements. For example, the updated standard for “students” incorporates requirements for academic and co-curricular programs, as it relates to the student experience.

The commission’s leadership will now give its members several weeks to provide feedback on the changes, which will be considered for approval at the commission’s December meeting.

If approved, the new standards would go into effect in July 2026.

The Backdrop

Accreditors — which gatekeep colleges’ access to federal financial aid — have been in President Trump’s crosshairs since the 2024 presidential campaign, when then-candidate Trump vowed to “fire the radical left accreditors that have allowed our colleges to become dominated by Marxist maniacs and lunatics.”

ADVERTISEMENT

In April, Trump signed an executive order that aimed to force accreditors to remove any requirements related to DEI, as well as to make it easier for new such organizations to be approved by the federal government and for colleges to switch accreditors.

More recently, as was the case for the New England commission, the Education Department has sought to use accreditation as a tool to force some colleges to comply with the administration’s conservative goals and definitions of civil-rights laws.

In June, the department sent notice to the Middle States Commission on Higher Education that Columbia University had violated accreditation standards because it had not adequately responded to antisemitic behavior during protests against the war in Gaza. As a result, the department argued, Columbia was in violation of Title VI, which bars discrimination based on race, color, or national origin, including shared Jewish ancestry.

The Stakes

Two other major accrediting agencies have also sought to minimize potential conflicts over standards that include DEI.

ADVERTISEMENT

Late last year, the Higher Learning Commission , which accredits some 950 colleges across 19 states, approved new standards that excised the terms “diversity,” “equity,” and “inclusion” from its standards.

In May, the WASC Senior College and University Commission, which accredits colleges mostly in California and Hawaii, announced that it was enacting a temporary “stay” on requirements that reference diversity efforts.

The moves are, in part, meant to assure state lawmakers that accreditors are not compelling members to break state laws that bar DEI programs. The Higher Learning Commission, for example, is working with potential new member institutions in Florida and North Carolina, which have such laws.

Conflicts with state laws aren’t an issue for colleges from the New England Commission’s historical region. But colleges from anywhere in the country can now apply to be members, Schall said. The commission now has member colleges from the Republican-controlled states of Florida, Georgia, and Missouri.

ADVERTISEMENT

Schall said the removal of DEI language could also shield the commission from punitive action by the Trump administration.

The commission is scheduled to go before a federal advisory committee in October that will issue a recommendation to the Education Secretary on whether it is meeting federal regulations to remain in its gatekeeping role.

“Would a secondary consequence of this be, somehow to avoid some attack on us?” he said. “Based on what we’ve seen, they seem quite free to come after the accreditors with a lot of information that’s not quite accurate.”

title: These Colleges Won’t Be Sharing Revenue With Athletes. At Least, Not Yet.
content:
Division I colleges entered a brave new world this summer when they began making payments directly to their athletes. That ability comes as a result of the House v. NCAA settlement, an agreement that went into effect July 1, and that rewrites the rules of college athletics.

But several dozen institutions decided not to participate, at least for now. Those colleges — 54 in total, by Sportico’s count — opted out of the settlement, forgoing the chance to share revenue with athletes, as well as the agreement’s other provisions, such as caps on the size of team rosters and unlimited scholarships.

The reasons vary. But athletic directors reached by The Chronicle described wanting more time to implement procedures that would allow them to pay their athletes. Some also cited a still-uncertain but mandatory cost each college will pay to fund the new enforcement organization, the College Sports Commission. Others said they wanted to see how certain legal questions related to the settlement played out before they jumped in.

The hesitancy on the part of some campuses reflects just how much stands to change in a post-House world, as well as anxiety over institutional finances in a time of tight budgets.

Members of the four most lucrative athletic conferences are automatically bound by the agreement. But every other Division I institution has a choice: Opt in and follow the House settlement’s terms, or opt out and mostly live by the old rules. It’s a choice that they will be able to make each year for the 10 years the settlement is in effect.

None of the five athletic directors reached by The Chronicle ruled out opting in eventually. Uri Farkas, vice president for intercollegiate athletics at Northern Arizona University, said his institution plans to opt in next year.

“The first thing we needed to do,” Farkas said, was “right-size some of our rosters.”

The roster limits imposed by the settlement gave a lot of institutions pause. For many, athletics is part of an enrollment strategy: They draw students with the promise that they’ll get to play the sport they love at a high level. With the settlement looming this spring, some coaches told players that they would no longer have a spot in the fall due to the new roster limits. That didn’t sit well with the judge overseeing the case, so lawyers for both sides agreed that current players could be grandfathered in and that they would not count toward the new roster limits.

But for several of the institutions who had decided to opt out because they did not want to cut players, it was too late to change course. The University of Nebraska at Omaha had planned to take a more gradual approach to get its teams to the right size.

“We told our coaches over a year ago to start shrinking towards the roster limits,” Adrian Dowell, the university’s athletic director, said. They’re close now.

ADVERTISEMENT

Dowell also cited the unknown fee that institutions will have to pay to the College Sports Commission, a new entity separate from the NCAA that will oversee implementation of the settlement. Several athletic directors said they’d heard the fee could be in the tens of thousands, but they did not yet know the exact total. The College Sports Commission said in an email to The Chronicle that it had no information to share on administrative costs.

“It’s incredibly frustrating when you’re being told you’re going to have to cover some share of an expense that you don’t know,” Dowell said. He added: “It’s no one’s fault. We’re building this plane as we fly it.”

Adding to the uncertainty, some legal questions around the settlement are still unresolved. The University of Nebraska at Omaha enrolls a number of international athletes, particularly in hockey, its top revenue generator. It’s unclear whether and how international athletes can be paid for their name, image, and likeness, or as part of a revenue-sharing plan. Dowell said that was a factor in their decision.

Instead of sharing revenue with athletes, the university will give more money to athletes for academic expenses. These types of payments can be up to $5,980 per athlete per year, thanks to the 2021 Supreme Court decision in NCAA v. Alston.

ADVERTISEMENT

Athletic directors also worried about Title IX challenges. Colleges will likely give the most money to players of football and men’s basketball, the two sports that, along with women’s basketball, generate the most revenue. Some colleges are waiting to see how the inevitable lawsuits challenging that arrangement play out.

“I just don’t want to get sued,” said Tim Collins, athletic director at Eastern Washington University, which is also opting out this year.

For colleges like Eastern Washington, new administrative fees and payments to athletes will have to come from somewhere, and Collins wants to ensure that he can continue to afford scholarships.

“We’re the college athletics that everyone fell in love with,” he said. “We can’t lose sight of that. I’m just making sure that opting in, opting out, that those decisions don’t impact our ability to really sustain the opportunities we have in college athletics.”

ADVERTISEMENT

Matt Billings, Portland State University’s athletic director, gave similar reasons for opting out this year.

“We have to pinch pennies,” Billings said. “I think everyone just had heartburn with not knowing all of the details.”

The athletic directors at Portland State, Eastern Washington, Omaha, and Northern Arizona all said they expect to opt in eventually and likely next year. At the University of North Carolina at Asheville, Janet Cone is not yet sure what her institution will decide. She said that her donors were happy to give money for athletic scholarships, but some were hesitant about contributing to payments for athletes’ name, image, and likeness.

“We’re not saying never,” she said of the decision. “We’re going to see how it plays out.”

title: In a Plot Twist, George Mason’s Politically Embattled President Gets a Raise
content:
George Mason University’s Board of Visitors gave Gregory Washington, its politically embattled president, a raise Friday amid a series of federal investigations over his efforts to racially diversify its faculty ranks.

Washington has come under attack by the Trump administration for the university’s response to the 2020 George Floyd protests, when students demanded that college leaders be more proactive in fighting racism on campus.

Many expected the board to fire Washington. Last month, James E. Ryan, the University of Virginia’s president, resigned over similar allegations.

The board gave no comment after two hours in closed session. Washington’s new salary will be $823,452.23, a 1.5-percent raise, and appeared to be part of an annual review.

“Regardless of how one views the events unfolding at George Mason University, today’s display of unity by the Mason community is inspiring,” Washington said in a statement. “It is a reminder of how centrally important our university is to northern Virginia’s families and economy. For now, the community can refocus on what really matters most: In just three weeks, we will welcome the incoming Class of 2025, which is once again the largest, most diverse and one of the most qualified freshman classes in the history of George Mason. Fellow Patriots, you are simply the best. Let’s get back to work.”

Dozens of faculty in attendance applauded after the vote.

James H. Finkelstein, a professor emeritus of public policy at the Schar School of Policy and Government at George Mason who has supported the university’s diversity efforts, said Washington is not yet out of the woods.

“I’m sad and disappointed,” Finkelstein said. “I would have hoped that the board would have given some more encouraging words about the president. This is by far the lowest base-salary raise that he’s received … I would read that as the board not expressing a high level of confidence.”

Washington, a former engineering dean at the University of California at Irvine, was hired in January 2020 as the research university’s first Black president. (The Chronicle’s publisher, who does not have a role in journalistic decisions, served on the board from 2019 to 2023.)

As the campus grew and rapidly diversified, he established a Task Force on Anti-Racism and Inclusive Excellence. While just 30 percent of its student body is white, according to 2023 data from the Integrated Postsecondary Education Data System, almost 60 percent of George Mason’s faculty is white.

ADVERTISEMENT

Like many college presidents in the last several years, Washington theorized that the university could improve its campus climate, tamp down on discrimination complaints, and increase graduation rates with a more ethnically diverse faculty. George Mason is Virginia’s largest public university and is deemed by the federal government a minority-serving institution.

Last month, the Department of Education’s Office for Civil Rights opened two investigations that alleged administrators made Jewish students and faculty feel unsafe during the Israel-Gaza war protests, and another two investigations were opened by the Justice Department regarding allegations that Washington and his staff discriminated against white faculty and students in their hiring and admissions practices.

Several faculty members have shown support for Washington in statements and social-media posts. They have pointed out that he was following directives for diversifying the campus and faculty that were put in place by the board years before his hiring at the university.

“When you are a diverse institution, you have to operate from that diverse framework,” Washington said in an interview with The Chronicle shortly after the investigations began. “I don’t run away from that. I run toward it.”

ADVERTISEMENT

A letter from the Justice Department claims that Washington instructed his staff to ensure that more faculty of color and women were hired and, in a 2022 social-media post, celebrated a faculty member’s work in advancing diversity efforts.

On Thursday, the Wall Street Journal published a 2021 letter from Washington in which he’d called on the university community to adopt “a broader, shared understanding of what ‘best’ means when recruiting faculty and staff.”

“If you have two candidates who are both ‘above the bar’ in terms of requirements for a position, but one adds to your diversity and the other does not, then why couldn’t that candidate be better, even if that candidate may not have better credentials than the other candidate?”

At Friday’s board meeting, Washington highlighted the university’s theme for the year, Navigating Through Rough Waters, and described the volatile campus climate he encountered when he was hired in 2020. “Especially at this time, it is incredibly important that we understand context,” he said.

ADVERTISEMENT

A week before he arrived in July 2020, protesters demanded that university leaders tear down the statue of George Mason, who’d enslaved 300 Black people. (A memorial to the slaves was constructed around the statue in 2022.)

“I want to be sure we understand the magnitude of what was happening on our campus in the aftermath of the murder of George Floyd,” Washington said at Friday’s board meeting. “We were really struggling with how to let the broader community know what was happening here.”

Washington previously pointed out that he was following a 2021 Virginia law that required universities to have “diversity, equity, and inclusion” goals in their mission, operations, programs, and infrastructure.

On Friday he told the board that, under his leadership, George Mason improved its rankings, built up its research, and resolved its fiscal debt.

ADVERTISEMENT

“This institution is doing extraordinarily well,” he said to thunderous applause from faculty.

But the political tide since then has dramatically shifted.

An attendee holds a sign that says “Diversity is our Strength” during the board meeting at George Mason U. Charlotte Kesl for The Chronicle

Federal and state Republican politicians have passed 28 laws banning a series of race-conscious efforts administrators have used to recruit and retain students and faculty of color. The Trump administration has withheld hundreds of millions of dollars from colleges for participating in what they call “illegal discrimination.”

Virginia’s Legislature is controlled by Democrats (no anti-DEI legislation has been proposed), but its Republican governor, Glenn A. Youngkin, has declared that DEI is “dead.”

ADVERTISEMENT

Youngkin appointed all 16 members of George Mason’s Board of Visitors. Four of those appointments are being contested by the state’s Democrats in court. Those members were not present at Friday’s meeting.

During the meeting, the board passed a “Merit-Based Excellence, Student Opportunity and Freedom From Discrimination” resolution, which ends all race-conscious initiatives including hiring, promotions, scholarships, financial aid, housing, and graduation ceremonies.

“Today we will conclude a two-year discussion on the subject of DEI,” the board’s rector, Charles (Cully) Stimson, said. “Your board has spent more time with students and stakeholders discussing issues surrounding DEI than all of the other boards in Virginia combined. That’s the Mason way.”

Dozens of faculty and alumni rallied in the rain, holding signs that read “Hands Off GMU,” “Diversity Is Our Strength,” and “Preserve GMU’s Academic Freedom.”

ADVERTISEMENT

Almost all of the faculty members asked that their names not be published out of fear of being targeted by the Justice Department.

At the meeting, Washington, dressed in a blue suit and a checkered tie, appeared calm and collected and joked with the gathered pool of reporters before the session began.

He pointed to challenges ahead, including building more student housing and renovating its arena. In a jovial tone, he joked about athletic facilities that haven’t been updated since 1982.

Resolving the Justice Department’s investigations would require soliciting clear and unwavering support from the board. (The U.S. House Judiciary Committee has demanded that he appear for an interview to defend his diversity efforts.)

ADVERTISEMENT

“We have to put in place a process for managing that and moving through that,” Washington said.

He ended his presentation with an animated photo of himself with “thank you” in multiple languages.

title: An Open Letter From Arne Duncan
content:
C ollectively, our higher-education sector is the intellectual and economic engine of the world. It has hoisted millions of people up the economic ladder, driven advances in every field from agriculture and astrophysics to manufacturing and medicine, and contributed in so many ways to our collective wisdom and understanding.

All of us have a stake in the system: administrators, professors, employees who work in the field, parents and students who pay tuition, donors and alumni who fund scholarships and endowments, taxpayers who have invested trillions and trillions of dollars to build our universities and expand access to college, and communities that are economically anchored by institutions of higher education.

President Trump is putting it all at risk with his higher-education attacks. Modeled on Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán’s takeover of his country’s higher-education system, Trump wants to weaken a sector that has the power to hold him accountable.

Authoritarians succeed by dividing — collecting scalps to wave in front of cameras and bring others in line. As the University of Virginia shows, Trump’s weaponized Justice Department will circumvent laws it is sworn to uphold to serve the president’s whims. As Columbia University shows, negotiating with Trump is a losing strategy: There are no concessions that will protect Columbia from future extralegal demands.

As Harvard University demonstrates, Trump will cancel billions of dollars in crucial research activities for manufactured crimes. His indiscriminate attack on George Mason University — with four separate investigations — shows the lengths his administration will go to bring a university to heel. As the trans-athlete debate shows, he will demonize a tiny and vulnerable population with exaggerations and lies to stoke outrage among his followers.

Trump’s attacks on higher education come at a time when our leading economic competitor is spending more to outpace us in crucial fields like science, technology, engineering, and math. In fact, in 2022, China awarded over 50,000 Ph.D.’s in STEM fields, compared to 35,000 in America. Meanwhile, our world-class research universities are bleeding expertise as other countries recruit our scientists.

The only hope for higher education is total and unrelenting resistance to Trump. Every college in America and every stakeholder must join together and pursue every possible strategy — legal or otherwise — to stop him.

More than four million people work in higher education — a $600-billion sector serving 19 million students and their families. There are millions of wealthy donors and alumni whose investments in higher education are being diverted to protect and maintain federally funded research the Trump administration arbitrarily canceled. In this fight, silence is assent.

The Rev. Martin Luther King Jr. did not march alone. He helped launch a movement that brought millions of people into the cause of civil rights. Similarly, Columbia, Harvard, UVa, and George Mason should not fight alone. The entire sector needs to stand with them.

America’s 6,000 colleges and universities should launch a nonstop public-information campaign to parents, students, employees, donors, alumni, and the communities where they are located, highlighting the moral and economic threat this administration represents.

ADVERTISEMENT

Universities should use their publishing arms to expose the Trump administration’s corruption and destruction of the American Dream. His budget bill represents a historic transfer of wealth from the poor and the middle class to the top 1 percent.

Universities can show the impact of communities losing health-care coverage as rural hospitals close. They can highlight farms and businesses unable to produce without immigrant labor, the exploitation of public lands, and the victims of Trump-driven violence.

Trump’s new budget empowers the executive branch far beyond historic precedent or constitutional intent. And thanks to recent Supreme Court rulings, as U.S. Sen. Chris Murphy, a Democrat from Connecticut, explains, lower courts now have less power to stop him.

Most recently, the Supreme Court gave Trump the green light to effectively dissolve the entire U.S. Department of Education, in direct defiance of Congressional authority. Yet, the Republican-led Congress has fully capitulated. Our system of checks and balances is broken.

ADVERTISEMENT

Like every other sector of society, higher education isn’t perfect. It should do a better job of fostering dialogue among people with divergent opinions and should not shy away from fact-based debates about issues like the handling of anti-Israel protests, or race-conscious admissions programs. That’s how a healthy democracy works.

But we can’t have honest conversations amid Trump’s thuggish, immoral tactics. People across the political spectrum have an obligation to call him out. Today, Trump is making a mockery of core conservative principles like states’ rights with his egregious federal overreach. Yet, most conservatives remain silent.

In April, 150 college presidents affiliated with the American Association of Colleges and Universities signed a letter denouncing “unprecedented government overreach and political interference now endangering American higher education.”

That’s a good start, but I urge everyone in higher education, in the strongest possible terms, to stand up, stand together, and resist. This fight isn’t just about a handful of universities. It’s not just about higher education. It’s a fight for democracy. Trump has brought suffering to so many people at home and abroad — and he is just getting started. Only we can stop it.

title: Opinion | Want to Save Democracy? Teach Art History.
content:
I am just old enough to remember the 35mm slide projectors used in art-history classrooms of the past. As a student, I found the gentle, continuous whir of their ventilation systems calming. The soft click, phht that signaled the advance of slides gave lectures a nice, reliable rhythm. Not infrequently, a halogen bulb would die or a slide would jam, necessitating a pause in the lecture and the deft hand of a technician. Today, we are relieved of the practical inefficiencies of this vestigial technology. But there is one feature of the traditional art-history-slide lecture worth preserving, now more than ever: visual comparison. The practice of analyzing two distinct images side by side taught me how to think.

The room in which I took my early art-history courses was designed to facilitate visual comparison. Dual projectors, fit into the small windows of a boxy projection booth, beamed images onto adjacent screens at the front of the lecture hall. The physical and technical configuration of the space reinforced a pedagogical practice with roots in the magic-lantern shows of the 19th century. I cannot recall what the classroom looked like, only that it was always dark, so dark that the people around me were unidentifiable. Even the professor, positioned at a podium at the very margins of the room, was an indistinct, grisailled addendum to the luminous, absorbing screens on which all manner of art appeared. Plush black carpeting and acoustic panels on the walls dulled the ambient noises of people: the clearing of throats, murmured talking, the shuffling of feet in the hall.

The room had a womb-like softness that focused the eye and sharpened the mind. It brought things together and set them apart, in particular in the context of a slide exam, wherein students are presented with pairs of artworks, objects, or buildings and asked to work through a mental puzzle: Why, despite the many things that may differentiate them, do these distinct images appear together? The exercise involves putting the images into conversation and then tracking, through writing, that conversation’s spontaneous ebb and flow.

A jewel-encrusted 11th-century reliquary rendered in the form of a Catholic saint might be compared, for instance, with the gilded pages of an early Quranic manuscript. Despite the formal, temporal, cultural, and geographic distances that separate these objects, they both invest material splendor with spiritual meaning. The comparison invites connections across religious traditions and allows the student to recognize elements of familiarity in unfamiliar social, cultural, or historical contexts. It offers a lesson in finding coherence across difference. The point is not to collapse those differences but to draw meaning from them. The student must dwell on congruities and hard-to-reconcile dissonances, and in the process, practice holding distinct belief systems in tension.

The practice of analyzing two distinct images side by side taught me how to think.

Today, for a variety of reasons, the pedagogical practices of art history risk falling into obsolescence like the projectors of yore. What’s at stake is more than a disciplinary tradition. Visual comparison cultivates thinking skills that are vital to public life in a democracy, particularly in an increasingly polarized world. Within the classroom, comparing works of art based on formal characteristics encourages students to find meaning in the space where things that do not belong to together meet. This activity translates beyond the classroom as a lesson in pluralism, a way of engaging in the public sphere where people, who by nature act and think differently from one another, must coexist and work together to build a world in common.

V isual comparison has not yet gone the way of the 35mm slide projector. But art history faces a broader existential threat. External pressures, such as reductions in federal funding for universities, compound an already-tenuous situation. Longstanding financial pressures, declining enrollment, rising tuition costs, shifting student incentives, and diminished public support for higher education correlate with the contraction, consolidation, or outright closure of postsecondary art-history programs. Within universities, educational programs focused on the acquisition and generation of new knowledge that can be directly and productively applied in the professional realm overshadow curricula belonging to the liberal-arts tradition. Visual comparison, a cornerstone of art-historical training, does not present an obvious instrumental value. Yet its capacity to stimulate sustained, open-ended thought should not be underestimated.

Visual comparison cultivates thinking skills that are vital to public life in a democracy.

We are often told that the humanities matter because they cultivate critical thinking. But what does that mean and what is at risk when we fail to think critically? In her polemical 1963 analysis of the trial of Adolf Eichmann, a Nazi official responsible for the mass deportation of Jews to death camps during the Holocaust, Hannah Arendt argues that Eichmann’s willingness to enact genocide stemmed not from an innate wickedness, strong ideological conviction, or even stupidity, but from an absence of thought. Eichmann was not evil, argues Arendt, but rather a shallow functionary whose unthinking attachment to bureaucratic procedure and willful withdrawal from reality led him to commit evil.

Arendt’s posthumously published final book, The Life of the Mind, is an extended postscript to her work on the Eichmann trial. It is an inquiry into the nature and potential of thinking itself, and it asks whether thinking might serve as a barrier to evil. Arendt does not arrive at a conclusive answer to that question. But her meditation on thinking — which she describes as a search for meaning rather than a quest for knowledge or objective truth — offers a way of understanding what is at stake in the practice of comparing works of art. It prompts the question of whether thoughtfulness cultivated in the classroom inspires thoughtfulness outside of it. Did the way I was taught to think across unrelated images in my early art-history courses prepare me to avoid the dangerous trap of thoughtlessness?

ADVERTISEMENT

For Arendt, the search for coherence across difference is central to the pursuit of meaning in both private and public life, with the human capacity for metaphor as an example of that pursuit. When a rock in the sea, for instance, becomes an emblem of “endurance,” or old age is described as “the sunset of life,” we draw connections between things that bear no obvious resemblance. This kind of analogous thinking also underlies the work of the art-history student, who learns to make meaning from the juxtaposition of seemingly discordant works of art.

According to Arendt, such thinking also prepares us for public life, a life among many other thinking beings whose greatest commonality is their difference, the shared faculty of thinking for oneself. In her essay “Truth and Politics,” Arendt writes:

The more people’s standpoints I have present in my mind while I am pondering a given issue, and the better I can imagine how I would feel and think if I were in their place, the stronger will be my capacity for representative thinking and the more valid my conclusions, my opinion.

Analogous thinking helps us enter into a conversation with ideas and opinions that are unlike our own. And visual comparison is, quite simply, a method for practicing this habit of mind. It teaches us to sit with complexity and contradiction and to find clarity in their midst.

ADVERTISEMENT

Visual comparison is a rehearsal for navigating the polarities of contemporary political life. Immigration, abortion, vaccines, climate, guns: Although I cannot apply the logic of formal art-historical analysis to working through these issues, the practice of visual comparison at least gives me a sense of hope about the possibility of overcoming the fault lines they expose. If I can find coherence in the juxtaposition of a medieval reliquary and a Quranic folio, perhaps it is within my reach to find a meaningful point of connection in encounters with people whose worldviews differ profoundly from my own: to find common ground, the thing we can all agree on despite our differences.

“The School of Athens,” 1511, fresco by Raffaello Sanzio da Urbino Wikimedia Commons

T he art-history classroom is not always a place for quiet looking and reflection. It can also be a site of animated discourse. As a teacher, I expect my students to ask questions, voice disagreement, and actively participate in conversation with one another. In this context, the private process of thinking becomes a public experience. The classroom is itself a place where differing perspectives are brought into dialogue around images, objects, or questions.

Though not a depiction of an art-history classroom, Raphael’s “The School of Athens” — a staple of survey classes and, of course, many a slide comparison — embodies the spirited, public life of such a space. Unlike the darkened, womb-like lecture hall of my youth, this 16th-century fresco presents an airy, vaulted forum. Monumental arches meet with rigidly ordered columns, entablatures, and pediments to frame the robed bodies of thinkers: philosophers, mathematicians, scientists, and artists. No two figures strike the same pose. Some stand upright and impassive; others debate, gesticulating theatrically; still others bend intently over their work: measuring, reading, writing, pondering.

At the fresco’s center, Plato and Aristotle engage in a measured debate, with Plato pointing upward toward an ideal domain of forms and Aristotle down toward the realm of lived experience. Their philosophies, expressed in opposing gestures, are brought into visual balance by the symmetrically ordered architecture that frames them. Like “The School of Athens,” the art-history classroom is a place where divergent worldviews are brought into a kind of mutual coexistence and productive tension. For this reason, strange as it may sound, it offers a model for a political culture in crisis. The art-history classroom is not just a place to learn about art, but a place to learn how to think and act democratically.

title: Can Academic Freedom Survive the Surveillance State?
content:
T he government lawyer sucked his iced coffee to the dregs just as the mid-morning recess ended. With the click of a door and a swirl of black robes, the judge re-entered the courtroom, and all of us — lawyers, professors, journalists, concerned citizens, and the assorted oddballs who make a day out of haunting legal proceedings — rose to our feet.

It was the first day of a federal trial, in Boston, for a lawsuit brought by the American Association of University Professors (AAUP) and other academic organizations. The case contends that the Trump administration’s attempted deportations of noncitizens involved in pro-Palestinian advocacy — among them Mahmoud Khalil, a graduate student at Columbia University, and Rümeysa Öztürk, a graduate student at Tufts University — had violated the First Amendment and chilled the speech of noncitizen scholars.

As the first witness, a young philosophy professor, settled into the stand for cross-examination, the freshly caffeinated government lawyer, William Kanellis, scanned the courtroom. The jury box was empty. This was a bench trial: Judge William G. Young, an 84-year-old Reagan appointee with a genteel, avuncular manner, would serve as sole authority.

There are certain methods of lawyerly showmanship that may sway a jury but fall flat with a judge. Kanellis, as became clear across the two weeks of trial, has a flair for courtroom theatrics. He is prone to large gestures, such as a habit of reaching out his arms entreatingly to a witness while questioning them. A barely perceptible twang — “students” becomes “stew-dents” — further adds to an aura of telegenic folksiness.

Whether to please the learned judge, lull the professor-witness, demonstrate sympathy for the scholarly life, or pay tribute to some fondly remembered college class, Kanellis elected to begin his cross-examination on an unusually philosophical tack.

“You teach, among other things, about the philosophy of language?”

“I do,” said the witness, Megan Hyska, an assistant professor of philosophy at Northwestern University and a Canadian citizen who had testified that morning about how the detainment of noncitizen activists had led her to retreat from political speech.

“Continental school or analytic?”

“Analytic.”

“Analytic, so more Frege than Husserl?”

“Correct.”

“Very good,” Kanellis replied. Behind him, on the deep blue carpet that separates the bar enclosure from the public gallery, attorneys seated at long tables whispered, texted, and passed brightly colored sticky notes.

ADVERTISEMENT

Analytic philosophy is known for delicate, sometimes maddeningly scholastic, acts of distinction-making. These distinctions can be so vigilantly subtle that they risk being dismissed as pedantic. At its best, however, the analytic tradition opens our eyes to significant differences that we might otherwise glide by. The philosopher J. L. Austin, for example, in developing a taxonomy of different kinds of utterances, alerts us to how saying can be a form of doing, as in a promise or a warning or a declaration of war. Of the three noncitizen faculty members who testified at the Boston trial about how Trump’s targeted deportations of pro-Palestinian activists had led them to self-censor, two were philosophers of language, attuned to minute distinctions concerning language’s uses and effects.

As the trial wound on, it grew apparent that the Trump administration, insofar as it has a philosophical orientation, might be described as more continental in flavor. The government seemed resistant to making any distinctions at all. None, that is, save for a single bright red line, what the Nazi jurist Carl Schmitt named as the only distinction that matters in politics, that of friend and enemy. Repeatedly, in testimony from senior immigration officials and arguments from government attorneys, crucial distinctions were obliterated in favor of a coarse lumping-together.

U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement and State Department leaders described how investigative reports on noncitizen students freely mingled known facts and claims made on social media; how criticism of Israel was taken, via strategic conflation, as evidence of antisemitism and support for Hamas; even how, in the clandestine, interagency process through which lawful residents are deemed “deportable,” the distinction between saying and doing — that old hobbyhorse of J. L. Austin — is undone, so that by some terrible alchemy, protected speech becomes punishable action.

The sole distinction to which the government hewed throughout the proceedings was that between citizens, who have rights, and “aliens,” whose rights are, in the words of government attorney Ethan Kanter, “context-dependent.”

ADVERTISEMENT

There was only one slip-up. During the government’s opening arguments, Judge Young asked: “Do the public officials, the defendants here, agree that a noncitizen lawfully in the United States has the same constitutional rights under the First Amendment as a citizen?”

“Our position would be that the First Amendment does refer to ‘persons’,” replied Victoria Santora, a lawyer for the defense, “and that people in the United States share the same rights under the First Amendment.”

Moments later, she offered a correction: “I wanted to add one qualification to my answer to the question you posed at the beginning. I apologize if I misspoke earlier. But I do want to say that there are nuances to the First Amendment.”

“Like what?” Judge Young asked.

“I’m sorry?”

“Like what? What are the nuances?”

“The nuance,” Santora tried, “is that this context involves issues of national security, foreign policy, immigration enforcement.”

ADVERTISEMENT

Two weeks later, delivering the government’s closing arguments, Kanter was crystal clear. “The answer to the question of whether aliens and citizens have equivalent rights under the First Amendment is no.”

In testimony from senior immigration officials and arguments from government attorneys, crucial distinctions were obliterated in favor of a coarse lumping-together.

The plaintiffs were not permitted to play in court the full video of Öztürk’s arrest, in daylight, by ICE. But it’s safe to say that everyone in the room had seen it: the man walking up to her on the sidewalk and grabbing her hands; the masked agents circling her, pocketing her phone, stripping off her backpack, handcuffing her, and leading her to an unmarked car. “The answer to the question of whether aliens and citizens have equivalent rights … is no.”

I t is a feature of our intractable times that political conflict nearly always takes the shape of a conflict over the nature of reality.

ADVERTISEMENT

One of the central questions of the trial was whether the Trump administration is implementing an “ideological deportation policy,” revoking student visas and arresting noncitizens because of their pro-Palestinian views. The academic organizations suing the government infer the existence of this policy from several facts. First, there have been high-profile detainments of noncitizen students, like Kahlil and Öztürk, presumably for pro-Palestinian advocacy. (Öztürk’s only sin, so far as anyone knows, was to help write an op-ed in the Tufts student paper criticizing the university’s response to the war in Gaza.)

Second, the government has boasted about cracking down on campus protesters. After President Trump signed an executive order on antisemitism, the White House released a fact sheet issuing a warning to “all resident aliens who joined in the pro-jihadist protests”: “We will find you, and we will deport you.” In March, Secretary of State Marco Rubio confirmed that his department was revoking visas of students engaged in pro-Palestinian protests. To carry out this crackdown, the government redirected resources away from priorities such as narcotics, assembled a specialized team focused on student protesters, and relied on rarely used legal provisions to revoke visas.

In court, the government’s response was simple. They denied that such a policy exists. As for scholars who feared their speech might make them vulnerable to deportation, such worries, the government advised, reflect a compound of grandiosity and paranoia. Professors are smart, but they do not inhabit the real world.
