title: Advice | What to Do When Career Planning Feels Impossible
content:
For many academics, the flexibility of the summer schedule allows time for the sort of big-picture career planning that’s difficult to do during the school year. At least that’s what I observed when I coached faculty members last summer and the year before. What’s different this summer? The No. 1 challenge I’m hearing, across all disciplines and career stages: It’s impossible to plan for the future.

To seek out coaching is always, among other things, an act of hope. Taking that first step toward changing your professional life reflects a belief — however fragile — that you will be able to improve it. But this summer, many faculty members are feeling upended by factors well beyond their control — the sudden instability of research funding; the rapid internal changes to programs, staffing, and priorities in response to federal edicts; and the widespread distress and anxiety of their collaborators, research assistants, graduate students, and staff members.

How do you plan your future in such an unstable, unpredictable environment?

New circumstances call for a new mindset. Management theorists make a key distinction between complicated versus complex situations. It takes effort to sort out a complicated situation but the information to do so is available, and you can see obvious, predictable links between cause and effect. The opposite is true of complex problems: Information about how to proceed is hard to find, and causes and effects are unclear. The late Doug Silsbee, a leadership coach and author, described the challenges of a complex situation in his book Presence-Based Leadership: “Many interrelated factors … are unknown, and some things in the system affect other things in ways that are impossible to predict.”

The faculty-career landscape in higher ed has always been complicated. But the planning mindset and the skills that you developed to cope with that system may not serve you well in today’s very different and very complex milieu. Your usual strategies for exerting control — such as making to-do lists, plans, and timelines — will not work and may even lead to adverse outcomes.

There are no easy answers, and to suggest one would be to minimize the gravity of external disruptions to faculty careers, as well as the attendant anger and grief. As an assistant vice provost for faculty advancement at Duke University, I’ve been working with faculty members recently in group coaching sessions. And they are finding ways to move forward, supported by their peers in an open-ended inquiry. In what follows, I share some takeaways from our conversations in the hope that other academics may find the advice helpful.

Ground yourself in what you know for certain. The more you fixate on the unknown, the easier it is to lose sight of important realities. In our group coaching, we’ve explored many versions of “grounding” questions, and here are three that we keep returning to:



What do you want for yourself in five years, no matter what?

Later on, in looking back on this moment in time, what do you want to say about how you handled it?

When you find yourself worrying about the future, what are you not noticing that’s right in front of you?

The first two questions help position people in the context of their own values — the “no matter what” aspects of how you live and work. Situations change, but hopefully your values don’t. The goal here is to seek alignment between what you care about and what you do next.

The third question — on “not noticing” — prompts people to remember what they may have lost sight of in times of heightened anxiety. That might be people and resources who can support you, or it might mean folks in your orbit whom you have the power to help.

ADVERTISEMENT

Look to nature for inspiration. I’m not actually suggesting a walk in the woods (although it never hurts in times of stress). Nor do I mean this suggestion as some sort of vapid platitude. Coaching conversations are rich in metaphors because visual imagery and creative analogies engage the right side of the brain and help people generate new ways to think about familiar problems.

I’ve been struck by how positively faculty members respond in the coaching groups whenever we start moving away from common models for visualizing career trajectories — which tend to be linear (timelines), structural (ladders), and evocative of factories (“productivity”) — and toward models that are much more organic, complex, and forgiving.

For example, I recently coached a faculty member who felt blocked in creating a strategic plan for the summer. Inspired in part by an exercise in Tamás Járdán’s Coaching by Drawing, I invited her to draw her plan as a tree. I didn’t know how the suggestion would land, but it ended up shifting her perspective, as well as the energy of the entire small group. We ended up “talking trees” for two whole sessions. What did the “strategic planning tree” enable people to see — or remember — in relation to their careers?



Personal history, identity, and values (roots)

Hard work, determination, and focus (trunk)

Multiple directions, generated in response to the environment (branches)

Tangible contributions (flowers and fruits)

Larger impact (a single oak tree can help support up to 2,300 species )

With so much upheaval going on across higher ed, it might seem like a strange time for folks to sit around drawing trees. Playfulness, however, is one precondition for creative problem-solving. Fear, anger, and cynicism all shut down creativity, and it’s hard to feel any of those when you’re drawing a tree (try it). But keep in mind: This exercise is not about generating immediate answers to narrow professional dilemmas; it’s about gaining a big-picture perspective of your career.

ADVERTISEMENT

Find the paradigm or reframing that works for you. Maybe you’re just not the tree-drawing type. In coaching, different paradigms work for different people. The key is to identify one that resonates with you personally while also nudging you out of your ingrained way of thinking. I’ve worked with other faculty members, for example, who seized upon the “ Odyssey Plan, ” a foundational exercise in Designing Your Life, by Bill Burnett and Dave Evans . There are no roots, branches or flowers here — just an invitation to plot three possible futures for your career:



Your “expected” path. The story you’ve been telling yourself about where your career is headed.

Your “alternative” path. What you would do if the original plan is no longer an option.

Your “wild card” path. If you were completely unrestricted by time, money, geography, or other commitments, what would you do? In other words, what’s your dream future?

I know this exercise can be powerful because I’ve seen it work. For example, I once coached someone who identified a feasible and compelling fourth path, which ended up being a hybrid of his fantasy career trajectory and his established one.

In periods of great uncertainty, finding a way forward in your career requires more time, patience, and creativity. How can you access those things now? And who can support you as you consider and talk through your options? This is not a time for linear thinking or for “going it alone” (a strategy beloved by many academics). The more complex your career landscape, the more people you may need to call on to help you navigate your way forward. How you respond in this moment may determine whether you feel blown off course or en route to an intriguing new destination.

title: Advice | The Case for ‘Slow Teaching’
content:
Ask students about the campus learning-management system and you are bound to get an earful: They feel bombarded by LMS messages about due dates, meetings, and grades. Instead of reading the syllabus, they rely on alerts to tell them what’s due and when, which probably explains why so much college work gets done just before class.

I started thinking about how the LMS contributes to undergraduate stress last fall, after I noticed heightened student anxiety. I decided to sit down with my two undergraduate classes and ask what was bothering them. Students from a mix of majors and class ranks told me they felt overwhelmed by life. Far from being the best time of their lives, they said, college felt more like a hamster wheel of endless deadlines and stress.

My students identified many of the same mental-health concerns that writers in The Chronicle and other journals have been concerned with for at least a decade — academic, parental, social, career, and financial pressures. With a new academic year on the horizon, it’s worth asking what other issues might be flying under the radar: Are any of our teaching practices adding to their stress? And what can we do about that?

LMS systems, such as Canvas or Blackboard, are some of the most ubiquitous features of higher education today. As professors, we are encouraged to use all of the bells and whistles of our campus LMS and to have students do the same. In the case of Canvas, professors are supposed to use modules that break the syllabus into “manageable” chunks. Each module contains the day’s or week’s readings and assignments — with due dates attached, about which Canvas then sends out a stream of notifications. In effect, knowledge is parsed into chunks through the LMS, and students receive it as they might a TikTok notification or a text from their mother.

If a student is taking four or more courses — each with multiple modules — their LMS calendar soon gets filled with many, many entries. If they have notifications turned on, as most do, they receive a deluge of to-do messages. For those who turn off their notifications, checking their calendar is itself an anxiety-producing endeavor. (I looked at a student’s, and immediately felt my heart racing!) Modules mean most students aren’t looking at the syllabus independently and depend on pings from the LMS to remind them of what’s ahead in a particular course. Students told me that they tend to do the work an hour or two before class. (I imagine the use of ChatGPT and other AI tools aids in that habit a great deal.)

In short, the LMS prompts many students to take a very passive approach to their coursework — until the pings arrive, at which point they feel overwhelmed and paralyzed.

The generation now in college grew up interacting with constant notifications. The silence of the before times — the very notion of being routinely alone with one’s thoughts — is a relic of previous generations. Gen Z inhabits a different way of thinking of time, self, and knowledge. They are, as Jonathan Haidt has suggested in The Anxious Generation, the cellphone and social-media generation, and it is making them very unhappy.

Once they arrive at college, we add to the noise. The campus LMS trains students to see learning as a chore — something to do or dismiss as the notifications roll through the week. But there is a different approach, and I’ve been doing it in my own teaching with some success: Rather than bend to the relentless, fast-paced “reality” of the internet, let’s do the opposite in our courses and slow things down.

I try to create a quiet space both in class and in my students’ heads. I tell them I am trying to teach as a “ slow professor ,” inspired by a 2016 book on the subject. To teach as a slow professor, I explain, is to resist the pressure to speed through learning and rather to see a course as a story, or multiple stories. And I tell students that I’m trying to help them develop a sense of agency over their coursework, which can lessen their anxiety about it. In order to achieve those goals, I do the following:



I talk about pedagogy in class so that students know the intellectual reasons behind how I teach, including the way I use the LMS. I mention the articles and books that guide my teaching.

My use of the LMS is very sparse. I post the syllabus and take attendance on the LMS. For large classes I will also post grades online. In my seminars, I generally do not give grades during the semester, but provide lots of feedback on written work and give a final grade.

The syllabus on the LMS has everything in that one document: dates, assignments, readings, etc., so students can scroll down and see all of it in one place. I do not divide up course content into modules.

I don’t do notifications (i.e., students can’t even turn them on for my classes).

I do not have online discussion questions or posts.

I tell students to look at the syllabus on a Sunday for the week and to plan accordingly.

In seminars, students must write everything in a paper journal (unless they have relevant accommodations), including their midterm and final. Students use the journal to write their reflections on the material both in class and outside of it.

Instead of a final exam, including in bigger classes, I have students write a final reflection in class on an issue they learned more about, a concept they struggled with, or a reading they disagreed with.

Sometimes I print out copies of an article for us to read and discuss together in class. It has worked very well indeed. That can’t be the only method you use because students learn differently, but it is a good option now and then.

I check in with students frequently by asking them to do self-assessments and taking time to talk in class about how they are managing their time, work, and life.

I have also brought in a recent graduate (who is now in our Ph.D. program) who talked about how to tune out the LMS.

What do students think of my attempts to structure courses so that we all slow down?

ADVERTISEMENT

Based on my evaluations across different courses in 2024-25, they are on board. In their written comments, they praised the classroom as “calm and conducive to learning,” talked about having to “dig deeper, ask questions, and get into a habit of writing reflections,” and noticed that I was aiming to get them to think and write for themselves. Some students said they found the final exam, a “final reflection essay,” a bit scary, since the only directions I give are open-ended. That’s precisely because, as I explain in class, I want them to think about what they want to say, without hand-holding or extensive directions. The upside for me is that the final reflections, despite some students’ anxiety, are a delight to read.

I doubt students would have written such comments if I had not been very explicit about why I teach as I do and why I only minimally use the LMS. I have learned over time that being explicit really helps bring them into the class as a joint endeavor of learning. So I tell students directly that:



I have an arc of learning in mind for the course.

I emphasize writing in notebooks because that is what the research shows is better for retention.

I want students to associate the class with a journal and a feeling of paper, rather than drifting into the black hole of one’s phone.

Professors and administrators must think long and hard about how we are creating the very anxieties we lament. Contemplation is a lost art in education, and our students are crying out for help to deal with all the challenges they identify as causing stress. Silencing the noise of the LMS and creating more space for reflection in our courses would be good educational practice for whichever century we are living in.

title: Advice | How to Grapple With the AI Already on Your Campus
content:
Students need AI-aware professors. Part of becoming one means staying up to date on what generative AI features have been enabled on your campus. That is no simple task. You may not realize it — or you may be actively ignoring it — but your institution already has a slew of AI tools that have been quietly embedded into applications that you use every day.

Generative AI is now active in most campus learning-management systems (LMS), research databases, and accessibility tools for students, among other programs. And, no, that isn’t the result of some sly administrative backroom deal. AI arrived on most college campuses, not through intentional purchases, but via free upgrades. It’s a less-exciting plot twist but one that every professor should analyze because the risks are many and easy to ignore.

One stealthy update at a time. The story of how generative AI took hold in higher ed is far more complicated and troubling than students using a single app like ChatGPT. Countless campus vendors with existing contracts simply upgraded their applications to use generative AI features. This is troubling because updates to existing contracts don’t require a clearly defined decision-making process or go through shared governance. Which means that faculty members, students, and even administrators may not have had a voice or agency in the decision to integrate AI into existing college systems.

Kathryn Conrad, a professor of English at the University of Kansas, foresaw much of this when she penned her 2023 essay, “A Blueprint for an AI Bill of Rights for Education.” At the time, many believed that higher ed would intentionally buy AI-enabled applications for teaching, research, and operations. The idea behind an “AI Bill of Rights” was to ensure that all stakeholders had a say in the technology their institutions purchase, with an eye on ethics, sustainability, privacy, data, and copyright.

Instead, campus vendors transcended that by providing AI in a series of system updates to existing products. Here’s how it played out:

In 2023:



Microsoft releases Bing Chat Enterprise (later renaming it Copilot). This version is given freely to campuses with Microsoft email accounts.

Blackboard integrates AI into Ultra courses. Once it is enabled, there are no opt-outs for faculty or mechanisms to switch it off. Like many of these AI tools, these features suddenly appear via an update.

In 2024:



Canvas integrates AI and rolls it out for free to all institutions.

D2L does the same, even creating “agents” — software that can take control of your computer browser and do multiple tasks for you — within the learning-management system.

Google unveils Gemini for education and gives institutions that have Gmail accounts access to its Gemini suite. This most recently included free access to NotebookLM under existing contracts (and, yes, even Google’s Education Fundamentals tier that is fully free to students allows full access to Gemini).

Dozens of tools that use adaptive and assistive technology for accessibility are upgraded using generative AI to assist with reading, transcription, and vision. Again, it isn’t something colleges (or students) necessarily asked for — it simply arrives.

Many vendors providing database access for research to campus libraries upgraded their search tools using generative AI.

In 2025:



Most of the systems providing operations for institutions have AI features integrated within them.

Many vendors subcontracting for operations do the same.

In short, AI’s arrival into existing campus software happened in bits and pieces and went largely unnoticed by many. After all, who spends time looking at individual system updates? Outside of big tools like Gemini or Copilot, few of these updates require IT to enable them. You simply wake up one day to an email announcing the app that you’ve used for years now has a slew of AI features — without discussion, warning, or any sort of training.

Banning those tools from your classroom has gone from impractical to virtually impossible. While you can certainly limit the use of generative AI in tests and assignments, you’re not going to be able to ban students from using digital resources they already pay for in their student fees. So what can you do?

How to become an AI-alert professor. Some institutions are already putting out guides to help faculty members better understand AI features in existing campus systems. One standout example is the library team at Texas A&M University at San Antonio: They’ve put together a guide that identifies various AI features now active in the university’s academic-research databases. By understanding which AI features have been activated at your campus, you can make intentional decisions in using them.

The challenge, of course, is that those campus systems aren’t static — they change with every update made by ChatGPT, Gemini, and the like. While many AI features are free (for now), others require paying a fee to access even more advanced AI tools. It’s frustrating to spend time figuring out an AI feature within your university-provided system, only to find that its usefulness has already depreciated because of a new version from the company, or a better model from a competitor.

That’s what makes adopting or resisting AI completely impractical. How can you do either effectively, with a technology that changes this rapidly? The most you can do is try to be aware of each AI update, and determine what it does and how it will affect your teaching and research. Here are three suggestions:

ADVERTISEMENT

Conduct your own informal “AI audit” every quarter. Set a calendar reminder every four months to spend 30 minutes exploring AI features in the campus systems that you and your students use the most. Document what you find in a simple spreadsheet with column labels such as: System Name, AI Feature, What It Does, Student Impact, and Privacy Concerns, etc.

AI features don’t always announce themselves. Most are integrated in subtle ways that are easy to miss. Look for the following:



Names. Some vendors brand chatbots with specific human names to make them seem more familiar, while others will use generic titles like “smart assistant.”

Some vendors brand chatbots with specific human names to make them seem more familiar, while others will use generic titles like “smart assistant.” Icons. Other telltale signs that generative AI might be present include icons of wands, glowing stars, or lightning bolts. Vendors use such icons to communicate that something potentially magical is present. The idea is to sell AI as something more than a prediction-based machine process.

Other telltale signs that generative AI might be present include icons of wands, glowing stars, or lightning bolts. Vendors use such icons to communicate that something potentially magical is present. The idea is to sell AI as something more than a prediction-based machine process. Language. Quite a few AI features will use language to announce what a tool does. Look for the words “generate,” “create,” or “compose” to understand if a feature uses AI.

By taking a little time to create and update your own AI spreadsheet, you can keep track of these tech changes, which is handy especially if your campus doesn’t do so.

ADVERTISEMENT

Create a shared faculty resource. Work with like-minded colleagues across the campus to compile your audit findings into a shared document. Include screenshots of AI features and brief descriptions of their capabilities. Share this with your department chair, and your faculty senators, and ask upper administration for support to create easy-to-navigate AI guides and other resources that are open to everyone.

Carry this AI awareness into your course policies. Help guide your students in understanding which AI tools they will encounter in the LMS and other campus systems by clearly articulating what those features are in your course syllabus. Avoid posting course policies on your syllabus that take siloed positions that are unquestioningly pro- or anti-AI. Instead, focus on real advice about AI and set clear expectations when crafting syllabus policies or guidance for your students. Doing so will help spark conversations and normalize discussion about AI in your classroom.

I won’t pretend that any of this is easy. We’re dealing with the intersection of rapid technological change, vendor contracts we don’t control, and campus governance systems that move at a glacial pace. But doing nothing guarantees you will keep playing catch-up to tech updates you never asked for.

It’s not hopeless. Faculty members are incredibly good at adapting when they understand what they’re working with. We want our students and ourselves to make informed and intentional decisions about the technology in educational spaces. In that way, generative AI isn’t any different from your LMS or another piece of software.

Document the AI features you discover. Share the list with colleagues. Ask uncomfortable questions at faculty meetings about which AI features are already active on your campus and whether anyone is training the faculty to use them responsibly. The most realistic path forward is building awareness one conversation at a time.

title: Advice | 4 Steps to Help Your Students Read Like Scientists
content:
“Eating Cheese Before Bed May Cause Nightmares, Study Finds,” reported People Magazine this summer. The same research on food intake and sleep prompted this take from Time Magazine : “Is Cheese Giving You Nightmares?”

It’s an interesting study, to be sure — if only the headlines actually described it. Turns out, only about 6 percent of the study participants said that food affected their dreams, and of that small group, more of them cited sweets than dairy consumption.

Oversimplification of scientific papers, or outright misunderstanding, has happened since reporters first wrote about science. But with the addition of AI chatbots into the mix, things have gotten even more dire. As misinformation and disinformation proliferates, the ability to comprehend primary literature in the sciences is more important than ever. While decisions about nighttime cheese consumption may be relatively low-stakes, accurately understanding some scientific studies — on, say, climate or vaccine research — carry life-or-death importance.

As faculty members, we can’t control the accuracy of media coverage of our research. But we can teach our students how to read and understand scientific literature, so that when they talk about science — in their coursework or on social media — they do so correctly. And that means thinking more carefully about teaching strategies to build science-literacy skills. Here, I suggest four concrete steps to help your students read like scientists.

Start with an assessment. When you’re trying to improve how you teach undergraduates to read scientific literature, you first need a clear sense of their starting point. Spoiler alert: It’s not going to be the same as that of a graduate student or Ph.D.

In a course I teach on food and the brain at the University of Notre Dame, I always give students an anonymous “ knowledge probe ” at the beginning of the semester. Alongside questions asking them to rate their familiarity with various course concepts and terms, it includes the question, “What steps do you take when you read a scientific article”? My students tend to be seniors majoring in neuroscience or psychology, and the vast majority respond with some version of “I usually just read from start to finish.” Those who elaborate often say they look at the abstract first, and then read the whole paper straight through — skipping over all the confusing graphs and figures — and perhaps reread the conclusion to confirm their understanding.

Aside from starting with the abstract, the typical undergraduate approach could not be more different from how academics interact with scientific literature.

Experienced scientists typically first read a journal article’s title and abstract, then hop straight to the charts and graphs (Figure 1, Figure 2, etc) for an understanding of the story of the paper. If they choose to dive deeper, typically, they next read the introduction, focusing on how it sets up the context, and then skim the methods section, intuiting what to ignore about the procedures used and what to focus on to ensure that the experiment answered the question at hand.

The crux of the challenge of trying to get undergraduates to a point of fluency with scientific literature is this dichotomy: Novices tend to treat scientific papers as dense prose with a few complicated and dubiously relevant pictures; experts tend to treat the figures as the real story, with the surrounding words providing depth and context where needed.

After 12 years of teaching courses based on scientific literature, I have learned that novice readers struggle with three core challenges: (1) interpreting data on graphs, (2) discerning what matters in an experimental setup, and (3) establishing enough topical knowledge to contextualize the study. In assessing your students’ skill level, I predict you’ll often encounter those same three variables, and I have some suggested strategies for each.

ADVERTISEMENT

How to interpret graphs and charts. As an expert, you may be able to glean the substance of a scientific paper in just a few minutes of glancing at the figures — but consider: What are you actually doing as you glance?

This highlights the challenge — and importance — of deconstructing how we work as experts in order to teach those skills to novices. As instructors, we need to break apart the analytical moves that whirl through our minds instinctively and walk students through each step of the dance until they can execute it on their own.

To train undergraduates in that mental choreography, I’ve developed a series of questions to help them analyze the typical graphs they encounter in a science paper. Among the questions I ask them to consider:



What’s on the X axis (the horizontal line of a graph)? What is the unit of measurement?

What’s on the Y axis? What is the unit of measurement?

What, specifically, does an individual data point on this graph represent?

Given what we know about the individual data points, how would you describe the data on this graph?

How do you interpret the findings of this graph? What might this mean about the hypothesis being studied?

What questions might this data or interpretation raise for you?

The whole process — nine questions for every graph — takes a while. For simple graphs, it can feel laughably infantilizing to ask college students to walk through every single step. But, invariably, it pays off, as they build confidence and facility in interpreting graphical information.

ADVERTISEMENT

This technique works best if you start with a graph that isn’t particularly complicated. That way, you can introduce how the process works and build student confidence in answering the nine questions. In my courses, for example, I use a fairly simple graph that shows ghrelin levels (a hormone associated with an empty stomach and hunger) rising and falling over the course of a day, before turning to more complicated ones.

Try going through this process socratically a few times in the early days of your course to establish what good answers to each of the questions might look like. After that, you might occasionally ask students to work through the same set of questions in small groups in class or as low-stakes homework assignments. Eventually, you can push them to use the protocol more quickly and independently, and on increasingly complex figures. Your long-term goal here: Establish this sequence of questioning as a habit of mind they will use to understand graphs and charts in scientific literature, or graphical data in any form.

How to understand research methods. Better graph-reading habits would enable students to understand the data of most scientific papers. But to grasp the source of that data, they may need to read the paper’s methods section — which takes a whole other set of skills.

Early in their careers, science Ph.D.s are told to write the methods section in enough detail for another researcher to replicate the experiment . The result: a lot of very detailed methods sections, and a wide chasm between the goals of the paper’s authors and the needs of its readers.

ADVERTISEMENT

Scientists and experienced paper-readers tend to scan the methods section. They have a sense of which bits they can skim or skip entirely and which will tell them something important to grasp the study as a whole. For example, in an fMRI study, they know they don’t need to read details of the “flip angle” or the “coregistration” — they just need to understand the task that the study’s subjects were doing while their brains were scanned and whether there had been some intervention beforehand.

Undergraduates, however, often read in a forced march straight through an entire methods section and tend to treat every word as equally important. All too often, they either don’t grasp any of it or spend unnecessary time parsing the details of “buffer concentrations.”

Given that the excess detail in a methods section can cost novice readers a lot of time and headache, how do we help them discern what matters?

Just as scientists turn to the figures of a paper for clarity, so, too can undergraduates benefit from visual thinking. In my courses I’ve used a simple but smart solution from a 2011 paper on teaching undergraduates to engage with science-journal articles: Ask them to draw a cartoon of the methods section. This exercise requires students to figure out the most critical information and communicate it free of jargon.

ADVERTISEMENT

In class, you might first talk about the purpose of a methods section, explaining the differences between how scientists read it versus novices. Then ask students to draw a simple cartoon of the experimental procedure. Their cartoons could also take the form of a timeline, a flow chart, or a grid laying out the subject groups and experimental conditions that are being compared.

From this, they learn to prioritize information in a methods section. Some students turn out shockingly well-drawn depictions of the cells, organisms, or whatever’s under study. Other students initially miss the point of what’s central to an experiment. But helping them to discern that is the whole point, and it’s a skill that improves with practice.

How to contextualize the research question under study. After the charts and the methods section, the introduction is usually the next thing that scientists glance at in a journal paper. A good introduction lays out the background information for the study, describes any subfields that inform the work, and ultimately summarizes the paper’s hypothesis and approach. But unlike seasoned scientists who bring a rich network of knowledge to their reading, undergraduates may know little or nothing about the subfield(s) under study.

Visuals can help here, too. Try asking your students to draw a “concept map” based on the introduction of a science-journal article. This idea was also suggested in that 2011 paper I mentioned, and with good reason. The simple act of seeking out the core concepts of a reading, and drawing clear connections between them on a digital or physical map, engages students with the introduction in a way that a linear reading, or even memorization, does not.

ADVERTISEMENT

This is a low-stakes activity that can be done as small-group work in class or as homework (students can snap a picture of their concept map to submit on the course website, or create their map on a digital program such as Canva or Miro ). Some professors give highly structured guidance on this task, but I prefer to keep it fairly open-ended and grade only for a good-faith effort at completion.

Asking students to visually represent the connections they see between various topics and ideas is a practical way to help them build the richer networks of knowledge they’ll need as they proceed in their careers.

title: Advice | Should You Use AI to Apply for Jobs?
content:
Editor’s Note: Previously in the Career Talk series, our experts on doctoral-career counseling have offered advice on managing your job applications, looking for industry positions, negotiating job offers, and other career-planning topics.

Applying for jobs has always been time-consuming, emotionally draining, and frequently demoralizing. You send carefully crafted applications out into the void and hope to hear something — anything — back. For industry openings, each application probably represents a couple hours of work. For academic positions, the amount of time per application can be much higher. And yet, very often, the answer is … crickets.

Now generative AI tools promise relief. After all, why should anyone spend hours drafting a résumé or a cover letter when a bot can do it for you in seconds? And why bother when you know that employers are using AI technology to review your materials and even to interview you ?

You’re far from alone, however, if you’re vacillating about whether to take advantage of AI in a job search. Many academics have serious ethical concerns, not only about how AI is affecting the college classroom, but also about the major ecological impact of constructing energy-sucking data centers for this technology. Maybe you’re also frustrated by the added responsibility of having to design assignments that mitigate the use of AI. Or you’re suspicious of its actual value proposition . For all of those very valid reasons, you may choose to avoid AI tools as much as you can.

But for many job seekers in 2025 — especially those with Ph.D.s or advanced degrees trying to transition out of academe — the ability to generate application materials quickly seems like a gift. And it can be. But it comes with a catch, even if you set aside your ethical or social concerns. Because AI is not just changing how people apply for jobs, it’s changing what those applications look like, and what hiring committees do with them. And not necessarily for the better.

In a tough job market, such as we are in right now, candidates are told to “apply widely.” Some candidates take that to mean that they should be sending out hundreds of job applications each week. AI can make it all too easy to do so. But we would advise against that for Ph.D.s. That ease of effort comes at the cost of quality, voice, and sometimes even opportunity.

At the same time, there are ways in which AI tools can help you in your job search — so long as you are thoughtful and reflective about what you choose to outsource to technology. We will get to that last part shortly.

“Brainstorm” With AI on Your Career Options

For the purpose of exploring career paths, especially in industry, the bots can serve as a brainstorming partner and research collaborator. If you’re new to using AI tools in a job search, this is a good place to begin.

Assuming you’re open to it, start by spending time with an AI tool. Have a conversation with ChatGPT, Claude, or one of the many other bots about a research area in which you’re an expert. You may be surprised at how well the tool converses about complex topics. But to get to that point, you have to be willing to move past the fully public version of the tool (which is generally little more than a search engine) and create an account (which will give you access to more detailed results and allow you to save your chats).

ADVERTISEMENT

“Talk” with the AI tool about your work experience, your professional interests, and your career goals, and ask it for help in identifying industries, job titles, and companies or organizations that would be a good match for you. Here are some good questions to ask AI in the early stages of your career exploration:



Here is my LinkedIn profile/résumé. Can you help me brainstorm some jobs and industries I might be well suited for?

Where do people find jobs in X industry?

What are some common entry-level job titles in this industry?

What are people saying about this company?

What are the biggest employers/industries in this geographic region?

I really care about X topic. What are some companies and organizations that are working on that?

Some of the answers will be neither helpful nor relevant, but other results will be. And in this early stage, when you find yourself getting discouraged, an AI tool’s perpetually cheerful and almost-too-encouraging persona can keep you engaged and on track in a way you might struggle with on your own.

If you still have questions on how to use AI for this kind of research, your university’s career center can help. Its staff members are no doubt working hard to master AI tools, often with the support of professional associations such as the National Association of Colleges and Employers, the Graduate Career Consortium , and the National Career Development Association . The career center very likely offers workshops on using AI for career exploration, or has advisers who can walk you through it in a one-on-one meeting. They may also be able to suggest AI-based tools — such as Jobscan or Teal — to help you to organize your job search or help you understand how companies use technology to “read” your résumé. Be sure to take advantage of the campus-based resources available to you. They can also share the pros and cons of using AI in your search.

ADVERTISEMENT

Your career adviser will very likely tell you that the one thing AI cannot do is network for you. A bot can help you find people to contact or suggest phrasing for an email seeking an informational interview. But human connection remains the purview of humans, and it is more important than ever for actually getting hired.

How It Looks From the Hiring Side of the Table

Imagine that you are leading a job search. Three days after you post the opening, you find that you have already received more than 150 applications. Yikes. As you begin slogging through the pile, you notice that a lot of the applications simply don’t sound, well … human. But a good chunk of the applicants do seem qualified. You start to wonder if there are any tools to help you distinguish between them.

For hiring managers, AI has created a tidal wave of (often mediocre) applications — some of which don’t even come from real candidates. It’s small wonder that, in response, some employers have eliminated cover-letter requirements altogether. Others have turned to filters, AI tools, or time-saving heuristics that push thoughtful applications to the bottom of the pile — often because they don’t match the qualifications exactly. And though we’ve talked to a few hiring managers who claim to look at every single application, most of them don’t have the bandwidth to read everything they receive.

Minimizing the human role in hiring can remove curiosity and imagination from the process, whether a hiring manager is using a traditional “applicant-tracking system” (or ATS) or building a new set of AI tools to help with recruiting. An AI-heavy search very often works to the detriment of people with advanced degrees who may not look like the candidate the bot “expects” to see. In applying for industry jobs, ex-academics have long relied on hiring managers who could look at a Ph.D.’s somewhat unusual résumé and imagine (with the help of a good cover letter) what they might bring to the company. No bot can do that.

ADVERTISEMENT

As a job seeker, you have no control over whether an overwhelmed hiring manager uses AI to make their own job easier. What you can control is whether you choose to add one more obviously AI-generated application to the pile or to take a more — dare we say — humane approach that will benefit both you and hiring managers.

Dos and Don’ts of Using AI to Apply for Jobs

Don’t use AI to fully automate your job applications. That means don’t ask AI to create résumés and cover letters from scratch based on a job ad. It’s easy to understand the appeal of doing so, even to candidates who would never use AI for their scholarly writing. For many Ph.D.s, drafting résumés and cover letters for industry jobs doesn’t seem like meaningful writing. Even in applying for academic jobs, while the requisite cover letters are longer and more culturally weighted, there’s still a sense that the writing isn’t doing intellectual work — it’s just summarizing what you have already accomplished. Summarizing and synthesizing is exactly what AI tools do well, you might be thinking, so why shouldn’t I take full advantage of that?

Our answer: Because the very task of summarizing and synthesizing your work is meaningful. It’s the chance for you to connect the work you’ve done to the work you want to do. Writing cover letters and résumés helps you understand what you’ve achieved, what you’re good at, and what you want next in your career. In answering the question of, “Why me, and why this job?” you have the chance to discover things about yourself and your career goals — and those revelations can help when you get to the interview phase. If you outsource that writing entirely, you skip the insights that come with it.

ADVERTISEMENT

Also, you risk not sounding like a human in your application materials. And that won’t help your candidacy in the least.

AI tools can help in drafting your application package — but only if you use them intentionally and in ways that preserve your voice and support self-reflection, while making strategic use of automation. For example, AI tools are especially useful for tasks such as:



Reformatting a résumé for a different labor sector.

Translating academic experience into industry-friendly language.

Brainstorming the bullet points for your résumé.

But a bot shouldn’t replace you. Only you can really express your interest in a particular job opening, your motivation for applying, or your fit for the position.

ADVERTISEMENT

Do write (or ramble) for yourself first. Before opening any AI tool, draft a “professional narrative” in your own words. What’s the thread that runs through your work? Which problems excite you? What skills do you want to use? Your narrative needn’t be polished at this point. But writing it out — even roughly — helps you get clarity and gives the AI something real to work with later. If the blank page is overwhelming, ramble into a microphone or an empty Zoom room and create a transcription.

Do this stage for every opening you seek. Before you ask the AI tool to do anything, wrap your own head around what appeals to you about the particular position. Even if you are following the general advice to “apply broadly,” you should not be applying so broadly that you can’t do this for every application. If you find yourself applying to so many jobs that this step becomes unreasonable, that’s a sign to be more selective in your search.

Don’t use AI as a ghostwriter, but rather, as a collaborator. Instead of asking AI to write your cover letter from scratch, ask it to revise or clarify something you’ve drafted (or at least rambled into a microphone). Ask it to help you tailor your letter for a specific role. AI is great at rewording and summarizing, but less great at capturing what makes you uniquely you. You should never let it have the last word.

AI is also helpful in doing research on individual companies and organizations (including universities). But its sourcing can be thin, and it is prone to “hallucinations” (e.g., “making things up”). Make sure that you review any source an AI tool gives you to ensure it actually says what the AI claims, and use your own judgment about the source’s quality.

ADVERTISEMENT

Do invite critique and pushback. AI tools can give very helpful feedback but, by default, are too polite — bordering on sycophantic. An AI bot will often tell you that things you say and write are “brilliant” and “insightful.” That is not at all helpful when what you need is constructive feedback on your application materials. Prompt the AI to challenge your work with directions such as:



Point out any vague or generic phrasing.

Does this sound too buzzword-y or academic?

What parts of this paragraph are weak?

Do make sure your materials sound like you. AI-generated writing tends to sound weirdly formal or strangely chipper. Before you send any AI-influenced documents to a potential employer, you need to ask yourself some questions:



Would I say this out loud?

Does this sound like me?

Is it specific enough to matter?

If the answer to any of those is no, we recommend revising. In a world in which hiring managers are slogging through hundreds of applications, anything that sounds generic fades instantly.

ADVERTISEMENT

Do rethink what it means to “apply widely.” Yes, AI tools make it easier to apply to 50 jobs in a day. But that doesn’t mean you should. For Ph.D.s in particular, job applications have never really been a numbers game. Given the state of both the academic and industry job markets, it’s important to consider multiple career paths. But we still believe that creating thoughtful documents for a reasonable number of openings promises a better payoff than applying for hundreds of jobs with generic application materials. Reflective writing is hard and tiring, but in a sea of bland, AI-generated cover letters, it will make you stand out.

Yes, job applications are a slog. But they are also an invitation to ask yourself: What have I done? What do I want? Where am I going? You won’t get useful answers to those questions from ChatGPT. And in a job market that already feels impersonal and opaque, self-reflection may be the only thing keeping you grounded.

Go ahead and use AI tools to make the search process more streamlined and less soul-crushing, but never surrender your own thinking to a bot’s. Your mind is still the most valuable thing you bring to the table, and you want it on full display to our beleaguered hiring manager, not buried beneath layers of AI-generated prose.

title: Advice | How to Convince More Readers that Your Ideas Matter
content:
Next year marks the 25th anniversary of Barbara Ehrenreich’s Nickel and Dimed: On (Not) Getting By in America, her best-selling account of attempting to survive on low-wage jobs. Writerly experiments in playing at poverty have always been controversial yet, without question, have produced powerful books that have illuminated life on society’s margins. Two key decisions Ehrenreich made in constructing her book offer lessons for academic writers seeking to expand the audience for their research.

Producing a bestseller that’s as successful as Nickel and Dimed might seem like too big of a reach. But as an academic with aspirations to write for the public, you can broaden your readership by following a principle I am presenting in a three-part series: Write like you teach . In Part 1, I described how to draw from an overlooked feature of the college syllabus — the learning objectives — to shape your writing in ways that will attract a larger pool of readers.

Here in Part 2, I turn to two key features of books like Nickel and Dimed — an experimental structure and a broad definition of evidence — that also happen to be characteristic of good teaching. Both features deserve more attention from academic writers.

Play with narrative structure. In the years after the Welfare Reform Act of 1996 , many people were entering or re-entering the work force and trying to make a living on minimum-wage jobs, often while managing health and addiction crises and facing barriers because of race or gender. In the opening pages of her book, Ehrenreich describes a conversation with an editor in which she wondered: “How does anyone live on the wages available to the unskilled?”

Thus was born Nickel and Dimed, and from it we can see one alternative to the information-dump approach of most academic books and essays. It’s a narrative structure known as “the quest.”

Ehrenreich could easily have conducted her life experiments in poverty, supplemented them with traditional research on economics and politics, and then produced a typical lecture in print, with one big idea or argument and many supporting examples. Instead, she invites the reader to peer over her shoulder as she seeks answers to the book’s driving question. By doing so, she presents herself as a curious person — a learner — rather than as an expert armed with all of the answers.

Good teachers present themselves the same way in the classroom. You certainly want students to know that you have developed expertise through long study, but you also want them to know that you don’t know everything, are still curious, and want to learn more. To that end, you experiment with teaching strategies, travel to conferences, and learn from how students respond to your courses.

Those activities are ongoing in your writing, too. But in documenting their scholarly quest, academics tend to share the results, not the journey. Making the choice to relive your scholarly quest in prose — to invite your readers along as you learn, as Ehrenreich did — will have more appeal than just drafting a long scholarly monologue on your findings.

Comb through some of your favorite nonfiction books, and you might discover they are powered by a quest structure. If you are a fan of the great work of Helen Sword, for example, you’ll see quest language in the opening pages of her book on scholarly writing, Air & Light & Time & Space : “When I first set out to write a book about the writing habits of successful academics, I had no real idea what I would find — or even what I was trying to find out.”

Most academic writing follows one of two narrative models: argument-based or information presentation. I’m not suggesting that you should always avoid those two structures, as they may well suit the audience and topic of a particular writing project. A good example is The Devil in the White City, Erik Larson’s historical-nonfiction account of a serial killer and the 1893 World’s Fair. Will editors be open to your narrative experiments? Many will. But it’s worth noting that, as you move further and further afield from typical structures, some skeptical editors might encourage you to rein it in. Their wisdom is always worth heeding. The effort is not wasted: Experimenting with narrative models can spur creative thinking about the shape of your writing project, even if the final form morphs back into a conventional structure.

Expand your definition of “evidence.” The faculty tendency to get locked into traditional modes of academic writing often carries over to the types of evidence we’re willing to use to support our ideas. Every discipline has evidentiary traditions that inform how Ph.D.s present ideas to one another. Sticking to those traditions makes sense when you are speaking to people within your disciplinary orbit, but moving beyond it to attract more readers requires a broader evidentiary palette.

You do that already in the classroom if your lectures and presentations include a mix of words, audio, video, and graphics. The text you put on a slide or a handout is the most typical form of evidence and might reach the most students, but for others, the key that unlocks their understanding could be a photo, a video, a graph, or a table.

It’s not a big leap to adapt that pedagogical strategy to your writing, and some academics have expanded the reach of their scholarship by offering readers a broader mix of evidence.

Eve L. Ewing, an associate professor and sociologist at the University of Chicago, adeptly offered multiple forms of evidence in her 2018 book , Ghosts in the Schoolyard: Racism and School Closings on Chicago’s South Side. The unrehearsed statements of a citizen fighting for the future of the city’s children matter as much to her argument as the statistical tables or the official proclamations of the Chicago Public Schools.

In the book, Ewing explained why she had filled out her traditional academic evidence with personal stories: “The experiential knowledge of people of color not only is a legitimate source of evidence, but is in fact critical to understanding the function of racism as a fundamental American social structure. So I cannot and do not aspire to tell you an objective story; rather I offer a story that is revelatory based on the experience of my own life and the lives of community members living in the shadow of history.”

Likewise in Nickel and Dimed, Ehrenreich fleshes out her historical, political, and economic research with the narratives of her own experiment, including many conversations with her co-workers at various jobs.

Such books demonstrate what effective teachers already know: Good research comes to life through stories, scenes, and conversations. Readers might forget the key statistic on page 53, but they’ll remember a compelling story that illuminated the point.

Drawing new readers to your scholarship, then, and convincing more people that your ideas matter, means pushing yourself outside of your traditional evidence boundaries. In writing workshops with faculty members, I try to lead them gently along this path. I usually present a long list of potential sources of evidence across many disciplines, including:



Personal anecdotes

Real-life examples from current events

Hypothetical scenarios

Case studies and biographies

Quotations from works of literature

Art works, images, photographs

Statistical tables, graphs, and charts

Outcomes from research experiments

Formal and informal survey results

Casual observations of events and people

Field notes (your own or from others)

Research and ideas from authorities in your discipline

Citations from academic research

Interviews with experts

Interviews with relevant subjects

If faculty members seem overwhelmed by the variety here, I ask them to select just one category and challenge them to incorporate that form of evidence into their current project. What would it look like to take field notes in a work of literary scholarship? To include personal perspectives from research subjects in a study of brain imaging from stroke victims? What kinds of readers would respond to those techniques? How might they reshape your thinking about the project?

Expanding your readership usually means expanding yourself as a writer, and that includes playing with both structure and evidence. You don’t have to write experimental novels about your scholarship or abandon traditional forms of evidence in your discipline. Just approach the work of writing as you approach your teaching: with a willingness to experiment, learn, and grow in the service of your learners.
